newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela's PDVSA cuts Maracaibo ship draught.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela's PDVSA cuts Maracaibo ship draught.

text.p: Venezuela's state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) has cut the draught limit for its tankers using the disaster-prone Lake Maracaibo shipping lane after a tanker scraped the bottom earlier this month, shipping agents said on Monday.

The channel has been subject to official restrictions for five months since a tanker ran aground and spilled 25,000 barrels of oil, but shipping agents say the silting of the channel has worsened recently.

PDVSA's latest cut, which follows similiar action by some international shipping companies, sets a 36-foot limit at high water, versus an official limit of 37-foot three inches. These compare with the normal 39-foot, six-inch maximum.
"PDVSA have sent instructions to their ships not to load beyond 36 feet. I was told last week on Tuesday," a shipping agent in Maracaibo told Reuters.
He said a tanker, the Nereo, sailed from the lake on about August 8 with a draught of 37 feet, three inches, but issued a report recommending a lower limit.

"She reported that when she went by buoy 23, her speed reduced from eight knots down to three knots and she took a sheer to port. Luckily she was able to keep some steerage and she stayed inside the channel, so she carried on to the States."

Shippers say the 36-foot limit will shave another 25,000 barrels from each tanker's maximum cargo in the lake, Venezuela's most prolific oil region. Tankers were already short-loading by 45,000 barrels on average due to the 37-foot three-inch limit imposed after a spate of accidents earlier this year.

Over one million barrels of crude oil are exported from Lake Maracaibo every day, mostly for the U.S. market. PDVSA is chartering more tankers and using Caribbean terminals as top-off points to maintain export levels.

Shipping agents in Maracaibo said they saw no quick solution for the dredging problem. Carlos Punar Abreu, former president of the National Dredging Institute (INC), was sacked in March, but agents report little change in the condition of the channel.

"The dredgers worked quite intensively for a couple of weeks, but ships taking ecosound traces can see there is still a huge hump. It's like a sleeping policeman (speed bump) in the channel," said one.
He said the Navy conducted a survey of the channel in May, but the results were not made public, despite several requests from international shipping agents.
"Last year ships were going out of the channel at 39 foot six and they were dredging the channel. Now ships are going out at 36 or 37 foot, it is allowing the channel to silt up," the agent added.
